posts.text: Tried running a meetup with no talks at all. Just three questions on a whiteboard and tables of six. People stayed an hour past the end time.
Every AI tool demo looks magical for 90 seconds. The real test is whether you still open it on day nine.
A small rule for community calls: the host speaks last. It changes who shows up the next week.
Wrote 400 words today that I will probably delete tomorrow. Still counts.
The best go-to-market plan I have seen fit on an index card: who, where they already gather, and what you give them first.
Sample thread: what running twelve small events taught me about turnout.
1. The invite copy matters less than who forwards it. A warm forward beats a perfect poster.
2. Pick a room that is slightly too small. Half-empty rooms kill conversation.
Is a builder community a product, a media company, or a club? Some days it is all three before lunch.
Shipping the ugly version in public was less scary than keeping the polished version in drafts for a month.
Onchain identity will matter when it saves someone a form, not when it earns them a badge.
Bangalore traffic has done more for podcast listening than any growth team ever could.
Reading list this month is all old books about new problems. Somehow they hold up better than the threads.
If your community only talks when you post, it is an audience. Nothing wrong with that, just name it honestly.
Using an AI agent to prep event run-sheets. It gets 80% right and the other 20% is where all the taste lives.
Indian founders are building for the next hundred million users with tools priced for the first ten million. That gap is the opportunity.
Monthly revenue update, posted publicly for the sixth time. The number is small; the habit is the point.
Hot take: most web3 events would be better as a dinner for twenty.
What would a newsletter look like if every issue answered one reader question and nothing else?
Morning pages, a walk, then email. Three weeks in and the walk is doing most of the work.
A photo from last night's session. Full room, bad lighting, great questions.

posts.text: Half the AI products I test are a prompt and a nice font. The other half quietly change how a team works.
Mumbai has the best informal tech scene I know: everyone is between two meetings and happy to grab chai in the gap.
